followUps:
A good answer is Observer for an order-status feature: when an order moved to SHIPPED, the email service, the analytics service and the mobile push service all had to react. Without the pattern, the order code would call each of them directly and need editing for every new consumer.

With Observer, the order publishes one event and each service subscribes on its own. We added an SMS channel later by writing one new listener and registering it, with no change to the order class. The price was care with failures: each listener ran in its own try/catch so a broken email service could not block the others.

Iterator. Java's for-each loop (for (String s : list)) is shorthand for calling list.iterator() and then looping on hasNext() and next(). Any class that implements Iterable works in a for-each, which is why you can loop over your own tree or range class.

Iterator<String> it = list.iterator();
while (it.hasNext()) {
    String s = it.next();
}

Python (__iter__/__next__), C# (IEnumerable) and JavaScript (Symbol.iterator) do the same thing.

code.title: Strategy picks an algorithm, State changes itself

followUps:
Yes, and it is common. A State object can hold a Strategy for one of its behaviours, because the two patterns answer different questions: State answers "what mode am I in?", Strategy answers "how do I compute this?".

Example: a vending machine has HasMoney and NoMoney states. Inside HasMoney, the price calculation can be a Strategy (normal price, happy-hour price). The state decides whether a sale is allowed and what comes next; the injected strategy only returns the number. Keep the strategy stateless so that switching states does not carry hidden data along.

Use an enum plus a transition table when the states have no behaviour of their own and only the legal moves matter. The whole machine then fits in one small, easy-to-read map.

Map<Status, Set<Status>> allowed = Map.of(
  NEW, Set.of(PAID, CANCELLED),
  PAID, Set.of(SHIPPED, CANCELLED));
if (!allowed.getOrDefault(cur, Set.of()).contains(next)) throw ...;

Choose State classes when each state has different logic (entry actions, different fields, different validation). With 5 states and 8 legal moves, the table is about 10 lines; classes would be 5 files.

code.title: Undo/redo with the Command pattern

followUps:
About 50 MB plus a small overhead per edit, if you store edits as commands and keep the text in a good structure. The command stores only the changed text, not the whole document, so one typed word costs a few dozen bytes.

Do not copy the 50 MB string per edit: 1000 snapshots would need 50 GB. Store the document in a rope or piece table so an insert only creates a few small nodes, and cap the history (for example the last 1000 commands). A rough budget: 50 MB text + 1000 commands x 100 bytes = about 50.1 MB.

Merge consecutive typing into one command. When a new character arrives, check whether the top of the undo stack is an InsertCommand that ended exactly where the new character starts, was made within roughly a second, and is not separated by a space or a cursor move. If so, append to it instead of pushing a new command.

if (top instanceof Insert t && t.end() == pos && now - t.time < 1000)
    t.text += ch;       // same undo step
else push(new Insert(pos, ch));

Typing "cat" then gives one command with text "cat", so one undo removes all three letters.

code.title: Safe Observer: snapshot, unsubscribe, isolate failures

followUps:
It lets a slow consumer fall behind without crashing it: the subscriber tells the publisher how many items it is ready for, and the publisher sends no more than that. In Flow, a Subscriber receives a Subscription and calls request(n).

Example: a subscriber calls request(1) in onSubscribe, processes an item, then calls request(1) again. The publisher never has more than one unprocessed item outstanding, so memory stays flat even if it can produce 1 million items a second. Calling cancel() ends the subscription.

Move to Kafka (or another broker) when observers live in other processes or services, when events must survive a crash, or when you need replay or many independent consumers at their own speed.

In-process Observer vanishes if the JVM dies; a Kafka topic keeps events on disk, for example 7 days, so a new consumer can read from the start. The costs are network latency (milliseconds instead of microseconds), delivery semantics (at-least-once means consumers must be idempotent) and operating a cluster. For a single app with a few listeners, stay in-process.

code.title: Chain of Responsibility: first-match and pipeline

followUps:
Chain of Responsibility passes a request along handlers that may or may not act, while Decorator always wraps one object to add behaviour to it and always delegates to it. The intent differs: CoR asks "who handles this?", Decorator asks "what extra work do I add around this call?".

Shape differs too: a CoR handler can stop the walk (a 401 response) and the caller does not care who answered. A Decorator never refuses to call the wrapped object by design, and the caller expects the same interface and result type plus the extra feature (for example a buffered stream wrapping a file stream). Middleware pipelines sit between the two.

Put it at the outermost layer, at the very start of the chain, so it wraps everything after it. In Express this means the error handler is registered last, because it only sees errors thrown by handlers registered before it. In a servlet-style chain it is the first filter, with a try/catch around chain.doFilter(...).

try { next.handle(req); }
catch (Exception e) { respond(500, "internal error"); }

If it sat in the middle, exceptions from earlier handlers (such as auth) would escape as raw stack traces to the client.

code.title: Template Method vs Strategy

followUps:
It is the rule "Don't call us, we'll call you": the framework (the base class) calls your code, instead of your code calling the framework. You fill in the steps and the base class decides when they run.

Template Method follows it directly: the base class method run() calls your overridden parse() at the right time. Servlets are the classic case: you write doGet, and the container calls it after setting up the request. The upside is that the order of steps is guaranteed; the downside is that you cannot change that order from a subclass.

Because the subclass part is not ready yet. When a constructor runs, the base class constructor executes first, so an overridden method runs before the subclass's fields have been initialised, and it sees default values (0, null).

class Base { Base() { init(); } void init() {} }
class Sub extends Base {
    String name = "x";               // assigned after Base()
    void init() { print(name); }     // prints null
}

The fix is to call only private or final methods from constructors, or use a factory method or an explicit start() call after construction. The same trap exists in C# and C++ (where virtual calls in constructors go to the base version).

code.title: BST in-order iterator with an explicit stack

followUps:
Add a second stack for visited values, or use a recorded list, and give each node a way to go backwards. The simplest correct approach is to keep a list of everything returned so far plus a cursor; prev() moves the cursor back and next() moves it forward, calling the real stack-based step only when the cursor is at the end.

if (pos < seen.size() - 1) return seen.get(++pos);
seen.add(stackNext()); pos++;
return seen.get(pos);

The cost is O(visited) extra memory, so the O(h) bound is lost. To keep O(h) memory, add a parent pointer to nodes and walk to the predecessor instead (O(h) worst case, O(1) amortised).

Keep a modification counter in the tree that increases on every insert or delete. The iterator copies it when created, and each next() compares it with the tree's current value; if they differ it throws ConcurrentModificationException.

int expected = tree.modCount;      // in constructor
int next() {
    if (tree.modCount != expected) throw new ConcurrentModificationException();
    ...
}

Example: iterate 3, 7, 9, insert 8 (modCount goes from 5 to 6), and the next call fails fast rather than returning a wrong order. It is a best-effort check for single-threaded misuse, not a thread-safety guarantee.

code.title: Mediator vs Pub/Sub

followUps:
Orchestration is the Mediator idea: one central coordinator tells each service what to do. Choreography is the Observer or Pub/Sub idea: each service reacts to events and no one is in charge.

Example saga for an order: with orchestration, an OrderSaga calls payment, then stock, then shipping, and calls the compensations if one fails. With choreography, Payment publishes PaymentDone, Stock listens and publishes StockReserved, and so on. Orchestration is easier to follow and debug but the coordinator is a central point; choreography has no single point but the flow is spread over many services.

Keep the mediator to routing and rules, and push real work back into the colleagues. If a mediator method starts doing business calculations, move them into the colleague or a separate service the mediator calls.

Practical limits: split by use case (one ChatRoom per room, not one hub for the whole app), keep it under a few hundred lines, give it an interface so it can be tested with fakes, and let colleagues stay usable without it. A useful check: if adding one new colleague forces edits in 10 mediator methods, it has become a god object.

code.title: Command inverse vs Memento snapshot
code.python:
text = "Hello"
print("start:", text)

# Command: store the operation and its inverse data (small, but needs a correct inverse)
appended = " World"
text = text + appended
print("append command:", text)
text = text[:len(text) - len(appended)]      # inverse: cut it off
print("undo command:", text)

# Memento: store the state itself (works for any operation, even non-invertible ones)
memento = text                               # snapshot before the change
text = text.upper()                          # upper-casing destroys the original case
print("uppercase:", text)
text = memento                               # restore the snapshot
print("memento restore:", text)

print("command stored", len(appended), "chars; memento stored", len(memento), "chars")

followUps:
By making the memento opaque: only the originator can read what is inside, and the caretaker (the history list) just stores it. Outsiders get a handle they cannot open.

In Java, make the memento a private static nested class of the originator (or give it a package-private constructor) so nothing else can call its getters. Store immutable copies, never references to the live internal list: copying new ArrayList<>(items) stops later edits from changing the snapshot. If the snapshot must leave the process, encrypt or sign it.

It does not undo anything outside the object that was snapshotted: sent emails, database writes, files on disk, network calls, or changes in other objects the originator only references.

Example: a memento of an Order object restores its fields, but the payment already charged at the card gateway stays charged. For such side effects you need compensating actions (a refund), which is a Command with a real inverse, or a saga. Also note that the memento restores the state as it was at snapshot time, so edits made after it are lost, including valid ones.

code.title: Visitor and double dispatch

followUps:
It is the trade-off between adding new operations and adding new types. In an object model you can add a new type easily (one new class) but adding an operation means editing every class; in a functional model it is the reverse. Neither style makes both easy.

Example: with 3 expression classes and 2 operations (eval, print), adding a Div class forces both visitors to get a new method, while adding a "simplify" operation costs one new visitor and no changes to existing classes. Visitor makes operations cheap and types costly. Solutions such as type classes or multimethods exist but need language support.

Choose classic Visitor when the set of types is open to outside code or comes from different modules or versions, when you need a library API that third parties extend with new operations, or when you are on a language or version without sealed types and pattern matching.

Also when a visitor must carry state or share traversal across several element kinds (like the Eval visitor keeping a result). Sealed + switch is better when the set of types is closed and in one place: the compiler checks every case is covered, and there is no accept() boilerplate.

code.title: Order lifecycle with State and conditional update

followUps:
Add a new OnHold state class and change the states that can reach it, leaving the others alone. In the State design that means two small edits and one new class.

class Paid extends State {
  String hold() { return "ON_HOLD"; }
  String ship() { return "SHIPPED"; }
}
class OnHold extends State {
  String release() { return "PAID"; }
  String cancel() { return "CANCELLED"; }
}

Decide whether ship and pay are legal while on hold (usually not, so they keep the default rejection). Add hold and release events, register the new state by name, and update the diagram and tests, including that SHIPPED still cannot go on hold.

Make the handler idempotent: processing the same event twice must give the same result as processing it once. Store the webhook's unique event ID and ignore ones you have already handled, and rely on the conditional update to stop double transitions.

INSERT INTO processed_events(id) VALUES (?);   -- unique key
UPDATE orders SET status='PAID', version=version+1
 WHERE id=? AND status='NEW';

If the insert hits the unique key or the update changes 0 rows, return 200 OK and do nothing more. Returning an error would make the payment provider keep retrying.

code.title: If/else ladder refactored to a Strategy map

followUps:
Write characterisation tests first: tests that record what the code does today, whether or not it is right. Without them, refactor in tiny steps and rely on the compiler and on comparing outputs.

Steps: capture real inputs and outputs (for example log 1000 production calls, replay them against the old method and save the results); then extract one branch at a time into a class or lambda; after each step re-run the replay and diff. Keep the old ladder and the new map side by side for a while and compare answers (like the program above) before deleting the old one. Commit after each green step.

A plain switch is better when the cases are few, stable, and all in one place, and when the branches are short. For 3 to 5 simple cases, a switch (or an enum with a method) is clearer than 4 classes in 4 files.

It is also better when you need to see all cases together, such as mapping HTTP status codes to messages, and when the compiler can check exhaustiveness (a Java 21 switch over a sealed type or enum). Use patterns when behaviour grows, when new types arrive often, or when the same ladder is repeated in several places. Do not add pattern classes for variation that does not exist.

code.title: Agent tool calls as undoable Commands
code.python:
# A model's tool call is just data: name + arguments
files = {"a.txt": "old"}
undo_stack = []

# Registry of known tools; each returns an undo action (the Command's inverse)
def write(call):
    previous = files[call["path"]]
    files[call["path"]] = call["text"]
    return lambda: files.__setitem__(call["path"], previous)

tools = {"write": write}

def execute(call):
    tool = tools.get(call["tool"])
    if tool is None:                                   # validate first
        print("rejected: unknown tool " + call["tool"])
        return
    undo_stack.append(tool(call))
    print("ok " + call["tool"] + " " + call["path"])

execute({"tool": "write", "path": "a.txt", "text": "new"})
execute({"tool": "rm_rf", "path": "/", "text": ""})
print("a.txt = " + files["a.txt"])
undo_stack.pop()()
print("undo write a.txt")
print("a.txt = " + files["a.txt"])

followUps:
Give every tool call an inverse or a snapshot, and log it before running it. This is Command plus Memento: a call is stored as data, and the host keeps what it needs to roll back.

For file edits, save the old content (as the program above does) or use version control and make each step a commit you can revert. For irreversible actions such as sending an email or paying, do not pretend to undo: require human approval first, or use a compensating action (refund) and a dry-run mode that only prints the plan. Make calls idempotent with an ID so retries are safe.

Because an explicit graph makes the allowed steps, the loop limits and the saved state visible, so you can test, stop and resume them. A free-running loop where the model decides everything is hard to bound.

With a state graph (plan, act, observe, done) you can: cap the cycles (for example 10 steps), mark terminal states, save the current state after each step to resume after a crash, insert a human-approval node before risky actions, and replay one transition in a test. It is the State pattern applied to the agent: illegal moves are unrepresentable instead of hoped away by the prompt.

code.title: Modern Observer with a closeable handle
code.python:
class PriceFeed:
    def __init__(self):
        self.listeners = []

    def subscribe(self, listener):
        self.listeners.append(listener)
        # the handle supports "with" and unsubscribes when closed
        return Handle(lambda: self.listeners.remove(listener))

    def publish(self, price):
        print("price=%d" % price)
        for l in list(self.listeners):      # iterate over a copy
            l(price)

class Handle:
    def __init__(self, close): self.close = close
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *a): self.close()

feed = PriceFeed()
logger = feed.subscribe(lambda p: print("logger: %d" % p))   # a plain function is an observer
feed.publish(100)
with feed.subscribe(lambda p: print("alert: %d" % p)):
    feed.publish(101)
                                                  # alert is unsubscribed here
feed.publish(105)
logger.close()
feed.publish(110)

followUps:
Back-pressure is the way a slow consumer tells a fast producer to slow down, so the data waiting between them does not grow without limit. You need it whenever the producer can be faster than the consumer for long periods.

Example: a sensor sends 10,000 events a second and a database writer handles 2,000. Without back-pressure the queue gains 8,000 items a second and the program runs out of memory in minutes. Options: the consumer requests only n items at a time (Flow, Reactor), a bounded queue that blocks the producer when full, or dropping or sampling events when that is acceptable.

Use a test listener that records calls, and assert on the recorded list. A counter in a lambda is the simplest fake.

List<Integer> seen = new ArrayList<>();
feed.subscribe(seen::add);
feed.publish(100);
assertEquals(List.of(100), seen);     // exactly once, right value

Also test the edges: after the handle is closed, a second publish must not add anything; and with two listeners, both are called once. For asynchronous delivery, wait on a CountDownLatch with a timeout rather than sleeping.
